questions.question: A 100 Ω resistor has 20 V applied across it. What power does it dissipate?
questions.explanation: Using P = V²/R: P = (20)²/100 = 400/100 = 4 W. The other forms P = VI and P = I²R give the same result once current is calculated (I = V/R = 0.2 A; P = 0.2 × 20 = 4 W). Knowing all three forms and recognising which to apply when only two of V, I, R are given is a core skill for this chapter.

questions.question: Three resistors of 10 Ω, 15 Ω and 25 Ω are connected in series across a 100 V supply. What current flows in the circuit?
questions.explanation: By Kirchhoff's Voltage Law, the total resistance in a series circuit is R_total = 10 + 15 + 25 = 50 Ω. Applying Ohm's law: I = V/R = 100/50 = 2 A. This current is the same in every element of a series circuit — a consequence of Kirchhoff's Current Law, which states that current is conserved at every junction.

questions.section_name: Basic Circuits — Resistors and Circuit Laws
questions.question: Resistors of 3 Ω and 6 Ω are connected in parallel and the combination draws a total current of 12 A from the supply. What is the supply voltage and what current flows through the 3 Ω resistor?
options: Supply: 24 V; current in 3 Ω: 8 A
Supply: 24 V; current in 3 Ω: 4 A
Supply: 54 V; current in 3 Ω: 18 A
Supply: 36 V; current in 3 Ω: 6 A
questions.explanation: First find the parallel combination: R_total = (3 × 6)/(3 + 6) = 18/9 = 2 Ω. With 12 A total, the supply voltage V = I × R = 12 × 2 = 24 V. In a parallel circuit every branch sees the same voltage, so the current in the 3 Ω resistor = 24/3 = 8 A. Check: current in 6 Ω = 24/6 = 4 A; total = 8 + 4 = 12 A ✓.

questions.section_name: Basic Circuits — Resistors and Circuit Laws
questions.question: A potential divider consists of R1 = 6 kΩ and R2 = 4 kΩ in series across a 50 V supply. What is the output voltage taken across R2?
questions.explanation: The potential divider formula gives V_out = V_in × R2/(R1 + R2) = 50 × 4/(6 + 4) = 50 × 0.4 = 20 V. The voltage divides in proportion to resistance: R2 is 4/10 of the total resistance, so it takes 4/10 of the supply voltage. This formula assumes no current is drawn from the output (unloaded divider).

questions.section_name: Basic Circuits — Resistors and Circuit Laws
questions.question: What is the equivalent resistance of a 12 Ω and a 4 Ω resistor connected in parallel?
questions.explanation: Using the product-over-sum shortcut for two resistors: R_total = (R1 × R2)/(R1 + R2) = (12 × 4)/(12 + 4) = 48/16 = 3 Ω. Note that the parallel combination is always less than the smaller of the two resistors — a useful sanity check. Here the smaller resistor is 4 Ω and the combination is 3 Ω, which is consistent.

questions.section_name: Basic Circuits — Resistors and Circuit Laws
questions.question: Three branches meet at a circuit node. Branch A supplies 5 A into the node and branch B supplies 3 A into the node. Branch C carries current away from the node. According to Kirchhoff's Current Law, what current flows in branch C?
questions.explanation: Kirchhoff's Current Law states that the sum of currents entering a node equals the sum leaving. Currents entering: 5 + 3 = 8 A. Therefore branch C must carry 8 A away from the node. This is a direct expression of the conservation of charge — charge cannot accumulate at a circuit node.

questions.section_name: Basic Circuits — Real Batteries and Maximum Power Transfer
questions.question: A source has an EMF of 12 V and an internal resistance of 4 Ω. For what value of load resistance is maximum power delivered to the load, and what is that maximum power?
questions.explanation: Maximum power transfer occurs when R_load = r (the internal resistance). Here r = 4 Ω so R_load = 4 Ω. At this point the terminal voltage is EMF/2 = 6 V and the current is 6/4 = 1.5 A, giving P_load = 1.5 × 6 = 9 W. Alternatively, P_max = EMF²/(4r) = 144/16 = 9 W. At maximum power transfer exactly half the total power is dissipated inside the source.

questions.section_name: Basic Circuits — Real Batteries and Maximum Power Transfer
questions.question: A battery has an EMF of 13.8 V and an internal resistance of 0.2 Ω. When it is supplying a current of 10 A, what is the terminal voltage?
questions.explanation: The terminal voltage is V_terminal = EMF − (I × r) = 13.8 − (10 × 0.2) = 13.8 − 2.0 = 11.8 V. As current increases, the voltage drop across the internal resistance (I × r) grows and the terminal voltage falls below the open-circuit EMF. This effect is why a battery that reads 13.8 V on no-load may sag noticeably when a transmitter draws a large current, causing power output reduction and possible frequency shift.

questions.question: A 100 μF capacitor is charged through a 10 kΩ resistor. What is the time constant of the circuit?
questions.explanation: The RC time constant is τ = C × R = 100 × 10⁻⁶ × 10 × 10³ = 100 × 10⁻⁶ × 10⁴ = 1 s. After one time constant the capacitor will have charged to approximately 63% of the supply voltage; after five time constants (5 s) it is considered fully charged. The time constant has units of seconds when C is in farads and R is in ohms.

questions.question: A 6 μF and a 3 μF capacitor are connected in series. What is the total capacitance?
questions.explanation: For capacitors in series: 1/C_total = 1/C1 + 1/C2 = 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/6 + 2/6 = 3/6. Therefore C_total = 6/3 = 2 μF. Capacitors combine in series the opposite way to resistors — the total is smaller than either individual value. In parallel, capacitances add directly (C_total = C1 + C2 = 9 μF for this pair).

questions.question: A capacitor is charged from a 20 V supply through a resistor with time constant τ = 5 ms. What is the voltage across the capacitor approximately 10 ms after charging begins?
questions.explanation: 10 ms = 2τ. The RC charging equation gives V_C = V_supply × (1 − e^(−t/τ)) = 20 × (1 − e^(−2)) = 20 × (1 − 0.135) = 20 × 0.865 ≈ 17.3 V. At 1τ the voltage is 63.2% of supply (12.6 V), at 2τ it is 86.5% (17.3 V), at 5τ it is approximately 99.3% (essentially fully charged).

questions.question: An inductor of 200 mH is connected in series with a 40 Ω resistor. What is the time constant of this LR circuit?
questions.explanation: The LR time constant is τ = L/R = 0.2/40 = 0.005 s = 5 ms. After one time constant the current reaches approximately 63% of its final value (set by the DC resistance of the circuit); after five time constants it is essentially at its final value. The LR time constant has the same interpretation as τ in an RC circuit, but it is the current (not the voltage) that builds up exponentially.

questions.question: An inductor with self-inductance 4 H carries a current that is increasing at a rate of 3 A per second. What back-EMF does it generate?
questions.explanation: The induced back-EMF is V = L × (dI/dt) = 4 × 3 = 12 V. This back-EMF opposes the increase in current (Lenz's law). The henry is defined by this relationship: an inductance of 1 H produces 1 V of back-EMF when the current changes at 1 A/s. A larger L or a faster rate of change produces a proportionally larger opposing voltage.

questions.question: An AC sinewave has a peak voltage of 325 V. What is its RMS value?
questions.explanation: V_rms = V_peak / √2 = V_peak × 0.707 = 325 × 0.707 ≈ 230 V. This is why the UK mains supply is described as 230 V — the peak voltage is about 325 V but the RMS value, which represents the equivalent heating effect of a DC supply, is 230 V. All quoted AC voltages and currents are RMS values unless stated otherwise.

questions.question: A square wave with a fundamental frequency of 1 kHz is analysed using Fourier techniques. Which set of frequencies is present in its spectrum?
options: 1 kHz, 3 kHz, 5 kHz, 7 kHz … (fundamental plus odd harmonics only)
3 kHz, 5 kHz, 7 kHz … (odd harmonics only, no fundamental)
questions.explanation: A symmetrical square wave contains the fundamental frequency and all odd harmonics (3rd, 5th, 7th, …) with amplitudes that decrease as 1/n. Even harmonics are absent from a symmetrical square wave. This is a direct consequence of Fourier analysis and explains why hard-keyed CW signals (which approximate square waves) produce strong spurious emissions at 3× and 5× the carrier frequency.

questions.question: What is the capacitive reactance of a 100 pF capacitor at a frequency of 10 MHz?
questions.explanation: X_C = 1/(2πfC) = 1/(2π × 10 × 10⁶ × 100 × 10⁻¹²) = 1/(2π × 10⁻³) = 1000/(2π) ≈ 159 Ω. Capacitive reactance falls as frequency rises — this 100 pF capacitor presents about 1590 Ω at 1 MHz and only 159 Ω at 10 MHz. At VHF and UHF even small capacitances become low impedances, which is why stray capacitance has a significant effect at high frequencies.

questions.question: An inductor of 10 μH is used in a tuned circuit at 14 MHz. What is its inductive reactance?
questions.explanation: X_L = 2πfL = 2π × 14 × 10⁶ × 10 × 10⁻⁶ = 2π × 140 ≈ 6.283 × 140 ≈ 880 Ω. Inductive reactance rises linearly with frequency — the same inductor would present 440 Ω at 7 MHz and 1760 Ω at 28 MHz. This frequency dependence is what makes inductors useful for frequency-selective circuits.

questions.question: A resistor of 30 Ω is connected in series with a capacitor whose reactance at the operating frequency is 40 Ω. What is the impedance of the combination, and what is the phase relationship between the supply voltage and the current?
options: 70 Ω; voltage and current are in phase
questions.explanation: Impedance: Z = √(R² + X_C²) = √(30² + 40²) = √(900 + 1600) = √2500 = 50 Ω. In a series RC circuit the current leads the supply voltage by a phase angle between 0° and 90° — equivalently the voltage lags the current. The angle is arctan(X_C/R) = arctan(40/30) = arctan(1.33) ≈ 53°. This is consistent with the resistor voltage being in phase with current while the capacitor voltage lags the current by 90°.

questions.question: In a series RL circuit, the RMS voltage across the resistor is 60 V and the RMS voltage across the inductor is 80 V. What is the supply voltage and how does it relate in phase to the circuit current?
options: 70 V; supply voltage lags the current
100 V; supply voltage lags the current
100 V; supply voltage leads the current
140 V; supply voltage is in phase with the current
questions.explanation: The voltages across R and L are 90° apart in phase (V_R is in phase with current; V_L leads current by 90°), so they must be added as phasors: V_supply = √(V_R² + V_L²) = √(60² + 80²) = √(3600 + 6400) = √10000 = 100 V. Because V_L leads the current and dominates over V_R, the supply voltage leads the current by arctan(80/60) ≈ 53°. Inductive circuits always have voltage leading current.

questions.section_name: Basic Circuits — Resonance, Q Factor and Bandwidth
questions.question: At the resonant frequency of a series LC circuit, which of the following statements is correct?
options: The impedance is maximum and the current is minimum
The impedance is minimum and the current is maximum
X_L and X_C add together, producing a large combined reactance
The inductor and capacitor values become equal to each other
questions.explanation: At series resonance, X_L equals X_C exactly, so their reactive voltages are equal and opposite and cancel completely. The only opposition remaining is the winding resistance of the inductor, which is small — so the impedance is at its minimum and the current is at its maximum. This is fundamentally different from parallel resonance, where the impedance is at its maximum at resonance.

questions.section_name: Basic Circuits — Resonance, Q Factor and Bandwidth
questions.question: A series LC circuit has L = 10 μH and C = 100 pF. What is its resonant frequency?
questions.explanation: f_r = 1/(2π√(LC)) = 1/(2π × √(10 × 10⁻⁶ × 100 × 10⁻¹²)) = 1/(2π × √(10⁻¹⁵)) = 1/(2π × 31.6 × 10⁻⁹) ≈ 1/(198.6 × 10⁻⁹) ≈ 5.03 MHz ≈ 5.0 MHz. This formula must be memorised for the Full exam. Note also the rearrangements: L = 1/(4π²f²C) and C = 1/(4π²f²L) for finding a component value given the desired resonant frequency.

questions.section_name: Basic Circuits — Resonance, Q Factor and Bandwidth
questions.question: A parallel tuned circuit operates at 3.5 MHz with a Q factor of 100. What is its −3 dB bandwidth?
questions.explanation: The bandwidth and Q factor are related by Q = f_r/BW, so BW = f_r/Q = 3.5 × 10⁶ / 100 = 35 kHz. A higher Q means a narrower bandwidth and sharper selectivity. The −3 dB points are at f_1 and f_2 either side of f_r where the circuit response has fallen to 0.707 (1/√2) of its peak voltage. The half-power bandwidth is therefore f_2 − f_1 = 35 kHz.

questions.section_name: Basic Circuits — Resonance, Q Factor and Bandwidth
questions.question: A series resonant circuit is driven at its resonant frequency by a 5 V RMS source. The Q factor of the circuit is 60. What is the approximate voltage that appears across the inductor?
questions.explanation: At series resonance, voltage magnification occurs: the voltage across the individual reactive components equals Q × V_supply = 60 × 5 = 300 V. This is sometimes called the Q-magnification effect. The same voltage (300 V) appears across the capacitor, but 180° out of phase with the inductor voltage — they cancel at the circuit terminals, leaving only the resistive drop. In a transmitter output stage at resonance, these voltages can reach kilovolt levels, requiring appropriately rated components.

questions.section_name: Basic Circuits — Resonance, Q Factor and Bandwidth
questions.question: A parallel tuned circuit has L = 50 μH, C = 200 pF and a coil winding resistance of 5 Ω. What is the dynamic resistance R_D of the circuit at resonance?
questions.explanation: Dynamic resistance R_D = L/(C × R) = (50 × 10⁻⁶)/(200 × 10⁻¹² × 5) = (50 × 10⁻⁶)/(1000 × 10⁻¹²) = 50 × 10⁶ / 10³ = 50,000 Ω = 50 kΩ. The dynamic resistance represents the high impedance that the parallel tuned circuit presents to the source at resonance. Connecting any external resistance in parallel with the circuit will reduce R_D and therefore reduce the Q factor and broaden the bandwidth.

questions.question: Compared with a well-made discrete LC tuned circuit, which of the following best describes the Q factor achievable with a quartz crystal?
options: Similar — both typically achieve Q values of 50 to 200
Moderately higher — crystals typically achieve Q values of 200 to 1,000
Significantly higher — crystals typically achieve Q values of 1,000 to 5,000
Very much higher — crystals typically achieve Q values of 10,000 to 100,000
questions.explanation: The Q factor of a quartz crystal is typically 10,000 to 100,000, far exceeding what a discrete LC circuit can achieve (practical LC Q values rarely exceed 200 in amateur circuits, and approaching 100 is already difficult). This extremely high Q gives crystal oscillators their excellent frequency stability and selectivity. Crystal filters in receivers use this property to produce very sharp passband characteristics.

questions.question: The equivalent circuit of a quartz crystal contains a series branch (L, C1, R) and a parallel capacitance C2. What behaviour does this circuit predict?
options: A single sharp resonance at a frequency set only by C2
Two resonant frequencies — one series, one parallel — that are within about 0.1% of each other
A flat impedance response across a broad frequency range
A resonant frequency that shifts by tens of kilohertz with temperature
questions.explanation: The equivalent circuit predicts two resonant frequencies: the series resonance of the L-C1-R branch, and a parallel resonance where C2 interacts with the motional inductance L. These two resonances are within about 0.1% of each other in frequency. A crystal can be used in either mode, but the oscillator circuit must be designed for the intended resonance — using a crystal in the wrong mode produces an incorrect or unstable output frequency.

questions.question: A transformer has 1000 primary turns and 250 secondary turns. The primary is connected to 240 V AC. What is the secondary voltage?
questions.explanation: V_S = V_P × (N_S/N_P) = 240 × (250/1000) = 240 × 0.25 = 60 V. This is a 4:1 step-down transformer. By conservation of power (neglecting losses), if the voltage is quartered the current is quadrupled — a secondary current of 1 A would require a primary current of only 0.25 A. Real transformers are not perfectly efficient (losses occur through winding resistance and core losses), but this ratio is a good approximation.

questions.question: An amplifier has an output impedance of 75 Ω and must drive a 3 Ω load for maximum power transfer. What primary-to-secondary turns ratio is required for the output transformer?
options: 5:1 — but the secondary must have more turns than the primary
The turns ratio cannot achieve impedance transformation — an ATU is needed
questions.explanation: The impedance transformation ratio equals the square of the turns ratio: Z_in/Z_out = (N_P/N_S)². Therefore (N_P/N_S)² = 75/3 = 25, giving N_P/N_S = √25 = 5. The turns ratio is 5:1 (primary:secondary) — more primary turns than secondary turns, stepping the impedance down from 75 Ω to 3 Ω as required. This is the key transformer impedance relationship: Z scales as the square of the turns ratio.

questions.section_name: Basic Circuits — Temperature Effects and Screening
questions.question: When placing an inductor inside a metal screening can to reduce unwanted coupling, what is the minimum recommended distance between the coil and the can walls?
options: Equal to the wire diameter of the coil winding
questions.explanation: The can walls should be at least 1.5 times the coil diameter away from the coil. If the walls are too close, the changing magnetic field induces strong eddy currents in the metal; these currents act as a lossy parallel resistance across the inductor, degrading its Q factor. At RF, thin aluminium or copper is used for the screening can; at audio frequencies, high-permeability metal (such as Mu-metal) is required to screen low-frequency magnetic fields.

questions.section_name: Basic Circuits — Temperature Effects and Screening
questions.question: A capacitor is specified as 'NP0' (also written C0G). Why is this type preferred over a high-K ceramic in an RF tuned circuit that must maintain a stable resonant frequency?
options: NP0 capacitors have a much higher capacitance per unit volume
NP0 capacitors have near-zero temperature coefficient, so their capacitance barely changes with temperature
NP0 capacitors can withstand higher DC voltages than high-K ceramics of the same size
NP0 capacitors have lower equivalent series resistance, reducing RF losses
questions.explanation: NP0 (Negative-Positive Zero) denotes a capacitor with a temperature coefficient close to zero ppm/°C — the capacitance remains essentially stable across the normal operating temperature range. High-K ceramics can have temperature coefficients of hundreds or thousands of ppm/°C, causing significant drift in the resonant frequency of a tuned circuit as the equipment warms up. For a tuned circuit at 3.5 MHz, even a 1 pF shift in capacitance can move the resonant frequency by several kilohertz.
